name: Spray-on hair

lead: Spray-on hair is a cosmetic concealer sold as an aerosol, shaker or powder. It either tints the scalp and thickens existing hair, or deposits tiny fibers that cling to strands, so thinning patches show less scalp.
It rose to fame as Ronco's GLH-9 in 1990s infomercials, and modern keratin-fiber products such as Toppik and Caboki follow the same idea.

paras: Users apply the product to dry hair after styling, matching a shade to their hair colour, and wash it out at the end of the day. Fibers are often fixed with a holding spray; coverage lasts until shampooing.
Products can transfer to pillows, hands and clothing and may stain in rain or sweat. Scalp irritation or allergy to ingredients is possible. It does not affect hair growth or the cause of hair loss.

angle.text: People use it to conceal thinning crowns, receding temples and parting lines before leaving the house. The effect is immediate and lasts until the next wash.

lead: Spray-on hair, nicknamed "hair in a can", is an aerosol or powder product applied to balding areas to make the scalp look covered [1]. It works by colouring the scalp and thickening existing hair, or by creating hair-like filaments that cling to scalp and strands [1].

Ronco introduced GLH-9 (Great Looking Hair Formula #9) in the 1980s-90s through late-night infomercials, and the company reportedly sold more than half a million cans [1]. Today's products include keratin-fiber shakers and sprays such as Toppik and Caboki [2].

Unlike minoxidil, which aims to stimulate growth, spray-on hair is a styling concealer: it improves how density looks and does not change hair growth [2]. Evidence is limited to product descriptions and anecdote; no clinical trials were found.

paras: Grokipedia describes three product families: powder fibers shaken onto the scalp, spray formulations with pigmented solutions, and hybrids with holding sprays [2]. Keratin fibers, said to be derived from wool or similar proteins, bind through static electricity, and plant-based variants exist [2].

Ronco pioneered the category as GLH-9, an aerosol sold on cable infomercials, and the founder Ron Popeil is credited with the invention [1][2]. The original was a liquid carrying powder particles that stuck to the follicles [1]. The documentary series Bald! included a participant who tried it with poor results [1].

Fiber products are discussed by hair-loss communities as a camouflage option alongside medicines and transplants. A T Nation user lists American Crew fiber among items in a gym bag, a hair-styling product rather than a fiber concealer per se [3].
Risks include staining, transfer and irritation; the product is a surface cosmetic and does not enter the hair shaft or follicle [2].

timeline.event: Ron Popeil conceives GLH-9 at Ronco [1][2].
